04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The message Fiona Bell sent the next morning was the closest Emma had come to a verifiable answer. An independent accountant had traced the follow-up reference from the authorisations book through the bank's surviving records. The first attempted payment had been returned. The subsequent transfer had gone into an account controlled by the Glenarraidh Education Trust, rather than directly to a student. Nevertheless, the exception entry had been marked resolved.

“That proves the student was never paid,” Sarah said.

“No,” Emma replied. “It proves where this particular transfer went. We still don't know whether the trust made another payment afterwards.”

A signed approval sheet attached to the reference bore Malcolm Vale's full name. The accountant had compared it with signed trust material from 2011. The evidence supported his authorisation of that transaction; it did not establish an intention to steal or explain every other grant.

For once, Emma could distinguish a documented finding from the allegation it might eventually justify. A case marked resolved in an internal register was not necessarily resolved for the intended student.

Another file arrived from Fiona in the afternoon. It concerned the later warning letter sent to Emma in Claire Morrison's name. An email from Malcolm's work account contained the letter's exact text and instructed a colleague to arrange its delivery as though Claire had written it. Emma and Sarah compared the original email record with the courier details and their copy of the letter. The wording and delivery dates agreed.

They offered Malcolm a right to reply. He acknowledged having arranged the letter, claiming he had wanted to prevent further distress to people involved with the trust. He denied misusing grant funds and insisted that the accounting questions had innocent explanations. Emma noted his position accurately without accepting it as verification.

That evening Fiona called again. Claire wished to speak with Emma privately, on the condition that her present location would remain confidential.

When the video connection opened, Emma recognised a face altered by fifteen years and a voice she had not heard since their café interview. Claire showed the original draft and booking details for the genuine letter written on 14 October 2026; Emma also checked private information with James Morrison. She would not publish the material used to confirm Claire's identity.

“The first letter was mine,” Claire said. “The second wasn't.”

She described leaving Glenarraidh on 21 September 2011. Daniel Reid had helped her travel away, but had not forced her into the car and did not know her current whereabouts. Claire said she had become frightened after challenging the trust's practice of describing authorisations as though they were payments received by students. She had feared consequences for her brother and for the young people she was trying to protect. Emma understood that Claire's account of those threats remained personal testimony, not an independently proven crime.

“So Nora really did see you get into the car,” Emma said.

“Yes. I made that choice. That doesn't mean I felt free to stay.”

Emma thought of the story she had written after Claire disappeared: a speculative headline about a private disagreement. It had wounded the family and distracted attention from the foundation's records.

“I treated an untested explanation as fact,” she said. “I'm sorry.”

Claire asked for two things. Her location must stay private, and she wanted to approach James herself rather than have a journalist arrange a reunion. Emma agreed.

The next day's article set out the verified banking sequence, the signed approval and the documentary trail behind the forged warning. It included Malcolm's response and called for an independent examination of the remaining grant records. A prominent correction withdrew Emma's original explanation for Claire's disappearance. The paper did not allege that every grant had failed, or publish the identity of Helen Ward's cousin.

James read the correction. He wasn't ready to forgive Emma, but told her he was glad the misleading headline had finally gone.

Her research log still marked the early anonymous calls and message as untraced. Reid's admitted omission required an official response, and the remaining student accounts belonged in the wider review. The article would make those limits clear.

In her Edinburgh flat, Emma placed Claire's genuine letter beside the published article. Not every account had been reconciled, and Claire's address remained unknown to the public. But the difference mattered: Emma had finally written what the evidence supported, and left the rest for the people whose lives it concerned.
